# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-36 (Extended v230)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 9, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba. **Timeline spanning 1821-1827 in Paris, 1814-1820 in Marseilles/royalist settings.**

## English Subplot Summary

**Established facts through summer Year 9**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Solemn promises: Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe.

**Chapter 34 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus.

**Chapter 35 migrations and events**: Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Kadan Corrley's journey to Salcombe postponed by flooded roads. Kadrek Brackick moved from Wilholt to Torton; Rinelle Corrley moved with him. Road rutted and puddled after thaw; light went early; frost silvered hedges; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; smoke lay flat over fields; wind carried salt and tar smell. Multiple characters hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Rovus, Ismira, Isric, Yewyn, Movus). Ismira fell asleep in chair before fire caught; Movus fell asleep similarly. Ismira laughed at story nobody else found funny (about salt price scandal). **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** Movus Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards fairly. Isric and Havie argued with carter over oat prices. Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family. Jotho Thornmere mended torn sleeve. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.**

**Chapter 36 (winter Year 9)**: In Ostcombe, Nerine Prydenridge hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. "The price of salt is a scandal" repeated by Yera Haskick to Rozek Stenenridge, by Rozek to Istho, and by Istho to Gadrek Prydenridge. Semor read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Gadrek Prydenridge laughed at story nobody else found funny. Tatho Brackick argued with carter over oat prices. Lurald Stenworth asked "Will it rain?"; Yera Stenworth shrugged. Yewyn Haskick spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Luvie Prydenridge remarked "I heard the river is up again"; Rozek said it always was in spring. Light went early. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Semor Brackick argued with carter over oat prices. **Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford.**

## Marseilles/Pharaon Ship Subplot (1784-1820)

**Edmond Dantès arrival and father reunion**: Young sailor Edmond Dantès jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Shipowner Danglars observed him disappear into throng. Dantès ascended four flights of dark staircase at Allées de Meilhan, found father training nasturtiums and clematis. Father unaware _Pharaon_ had arrived. Dantès told father Captain Leclere is dead; probable he shall become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits. Emptied pockets—dozen gold pieces, five-franc pieces, smaller coin. Money not his; was expressing fears. Said money at Caderousse's service if needed. Observed greedy glance in Caderousse's dark eyes.

**Fernand and Mercédès tragic romance**: Fernand begged Mercédès to repeat refusal; ten years of marriage dreams ruined. Mercédès replied she never encouraged hope; always said she loved him as brother; heart belonged to another. Fernand included in conscription, at liberty on sufferance. Mercédès poor orphan without fortune—half-ruined hut and ragged nets, father's inheritance. Mother dead a year; subsisted on public charity. Fernand pretended she useful, shared fishing produce; she accepted as cousin. When Fernand asked final determination, **Mercédès declared: if misfortune occur to Edmond, she would ascend Cape de Morgiou and cast herself headlong from it.** This calmness revealed to Fernand she read innermost depths of his sinister thought. His hatred rushed out of house.

**Edmond and Mercédès reunion and Fernand's threat**: Clasp in each other's arms under burning Marseilles sun. Suddenly Dantès saw gloomy, pale, threatening countenance of Fernand in shadow. Young Catalan placed hand on knife at belt. Dantès extended other hand with cordial air. Fernand remained mute and trembling. Dantès' anger waxed hot.

**Danglars' denunciation plan**: Danglars muttered he shall get nothing from these fools; feared being between drunkard and coward. Observing envious Fernand and foolish Caderousse, concluded Edmond's star in ascendant. Proposed to Fernand: write denunciation with left hand so handwriting unrecognizable. Wrote denunciation letter to king's attorney naming Edmond Dantès as Murat's agent carrying letters for usurper and Bonapartist committee.

**Caderousse's moral intervention**: Caderousse, after reading letter, comprehended all misery denunciation must entail. Exclaimed: "Yes, and that's all settled; only it will be an infamous shame." Stretched hand to reach letter; Danglars took it beyond reach, claimed jest, squeezed letter and threw into corner of arbor. Earlier, Caderousse said: "Kill Dantès! who talks of killing Dantès? I won't have him killed. He's my friend, and this morning offered to share his money with me."

**1814 wedding and feast at La Réserve**: As bridal party came in sight of La Réserve, M. Morrel descended to meet it, followed by soldiers and sailors. Had repeated promise that Dantès should succeed late Captain Leclere. Edmond placed arm of affianced bride within that of M. Morrel, who conducted her up wooden steps. Guests gayly followed; structure creaked under tread. Bell for vespers rang thinly. Feast chamber spacious and lighted by windows inscribed with names of principal French cities; wooden balcony extended entire length. Entertainment fixed twelve o'clock; hour previous balcony filled with impatient guests—favored crew of _Pharaon_ and Dantès' personal friends. All in choicest costumes. Mercédès, lovely as Greek girls of Cyprus or Chios, with bright flashing jet eyes and ripe coral lips, moved with light, free step. At table centre, Mercédès said "Father," pointing to father on her right; on her left she placed Fernand, "him who has ever been as a brother to me," with soft, gentle smile. Her words inflicted direst torture on Fernand; his lips became ghastly pale, blood retreated beneath dark complexion. Dantès' old father carried glass of topaz-hued wine to lips. Dantès explained: "Thanks to M. Morrel's influence, all difficulties removed. Permission waived usual delay; at half-past two o'clock Mayor of Marseilles will be waiting at city hall. Tomorrow he starts for Paris; four days to go, four to return, one to discharge commission, back by first of March. On second he gives real marriage feast."

**Arrest and Villefort's interrogation**: Danglars, observing Fernand's look, saw him stagger and fall convulsively against seat near open window. Indistinct sound on stairs, measured tread of soldiery, clanking of swords. Loud voice: "I demand admittance in the name of the law!" Magistrate wearing official scarf presented himself with four soldiers and corporal. Announced: "I am bearer of order of arrest." M. Morrel felt resistance useless. Old Dantès prayed and supplicated in terms moving even the officer, who kindly said: "Your son has probably neglected some prescribed form; more than probable he will be set at liberty directly he gives information required." Dantès surrendered, saying: "Make yourselves quite easy, there is some little mistake to clear up, that's all." Long terrified silence followed. Old father and Mercédès remained apart absorbed in grief; at length rushed into each other's arms. Fernand appeared, poured glass of water with trembling hand, sat next to Mercédès, instinctively drew back chair.

**Villefort's interrogation and Dantès' testimony**: Villefort traversed antechamber, cast side glance at Dantès, took packet from gendarme, disappeared. Dantès entered pale but calm, saluting judge with easy politeness. Villefort, impassive magistrate, demanded: "Who and what are you?" Dantès replied: "I was at festival of my marriage, monsieur," voice slightly tremulous. "I am on point of marrying young girl I have been attached to for three years." Villefort struck with coincidence; Dantès' tremulous voice in midst of happiness struck sympathetic chord—Villefort also was on point of being married, summoned from happiness to destroy that of another. When asked political opinions, Dantès replied: "Alas, sir, I never had any opinions. I am hardly nineteen; I know nothing; I have no part to play. I love my father, I respect M. Morrel, and I adore Mercédès." Villefort gazed at ingenuous countenance, recollected words of Renée beseeching indulgence for culprit. Every word young man uttered convinced him more of innocence. Simple, natural, eloquent with eloquence of heart; full of affection for everybody. **Regarding Captain Leclere's death and commission: "What I ought to have done, and what everyone would have done in my place. Everywhere the last requests of dying man are sacred; but with sailor the last requests of superior are commands. I sailed for Island of Elba, arrived next day; found difficulty obtaining access to grand-marshal; sent ring received from captain; was instantly admitted. He questioned me concerning Captain Leclere's death; gave me letter to carry to person in Paris. I undertook it because it was what my captain bade me do. I landed here, regulated affairs of vessel, hastened to visit affianced bride, more lovely than ever. Thanks to M. Morrel, all forms got over; I was at marriage feast; should have been married in hour, intended to start for Paris tomorrow, had I not been arrested on unjust charge."** Villefort said: "This seems truth. If culpable, imprudence in obedience to captain's orders. Give up letter from Elba, pass word you will appear if required, go rejoin friends." Villefort's face became joyous, thinking: "I hope I shall gain Renée's favor by obeying first command she imposed on me."

**Dantès arrested and imprisoned (1 March)**: Commissary made sign to two gendarmes, who placed themselves on Dantès' right and left. Door to Palais de Justice opened; they went through long range of gloomy corridors. Palais communicated with prison—sombre edifice with grated windows overlooking clock-tower of Accoules. After numberless windings, Dantès saw door with iron wicket. Commissary took iron mallet, knocked thrice; every blow seemed to Dantès struck on his heart. Door opened, gendarmes pushed him forward, door closed loudly behind. Air was thick and mephitic—he was in prison. Conducted to tolerably neat but grated, barred chamber; appearance did not greatly alarm him; Villefort's words resounded like promise of freedom. Four o'clock when placed in chamber; 1 March; prisoner soon buried in darkness. Obscurity augmented acuteness of hearing; at slightest sound he rose, hastened to door, convinced they were about to liberate him. About ten o'clock, steps heard in corridor, key turned in lock, bolts creaked, massy oaken door flew open, flood of light from two torches pervaded apartment. Through grating, Dantès saw they were passing through Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis to quay. Soon saw lights of La Consigne. Officer opened door without speaking word; Dantès saw passage formed from carriage to port between soldier ranks. Two gendarmes descended first; he ordered to alight; gendarmes on each side followed. Advanced towards boat held by custom-house officer near quay. Soldiers looked at Dantès with stupid curiosity. In instant placed in stern-sheets between gendarmes; officer stationed at bow. Shove sent boat adrift; four sturdy oarsmen impelled it rapidly towards Pilon. At shout from boat, chain closing port mouth lowered; in second they were in Frioul outside inner harbor.

## Marseilles Royalist Society and Villefort (1814-1820)

**Aristocratic gathering and political passions**: In mansion built by Puget in Rue du Grand Cours opposite Medusa fountain, second marriage feast being celebrated simultaneously with Dantès' nuptials (1814). Assembly composed of flower of Marseilles society—magistrates, officers, younger family members brought up to hate Napoleon. Guests at table; heated conversation betrayed violent, vindictive passions of South where religious strife gave bitterness to party feeling. Magistrates discussed political views freely; military talked unreservedly of Moscow and Leipzig; women commented on divorce of Josephine. **Marquis de Saint-Méran proposed health of King Louis XVIII, recalling patient exile of Hartwell and peace-loving King; toast excited universal enthusiasm; glasses elevated à l'Anglaise; ladies strewed table with floral treasures.** Marquise de Saint-Méran (stern, forbidding eye, fifty years old) denounced revolutionists who purchased confiscated possessions during Reign of Terror. Young, lovely Renée de Saint-Méran with light brown hair and liquid crystal eyes engaged M. de Villefort. **Villefort replied he would place Robespierre on scaffold in Place Louis Quinze and Napoleon on column of Place Vendôme; one equality elevates, other degrades; both revolutionary scoundrels; 9th Thermidor and 4th April 1814 lucky days for France. Acknowledged fallen Napoleon retained parasitical satellites.** Villefort's father was Girondin, later senator; Villefort laid aside father's name, disowned principles, became staunch royalist. **Marquise warned Villefort should be bound to visit offence with rigorous punishment against conspirators, as he belongs to suspected family.**

**1817-1820 developments and royal approval**: In 1817, Villefort made well-turned speech regarding father's abjuration and support of religion and order. In 1818, Comte de Salvieux cried that he said same at Tuileries when questioned by king's chamberlain. King overheard, interrupted: 'Villefort—is young man of great judgment and discretion, sure to make figure in profession; I like him much; pleased he becomes son-in-law of Marquis de Saint-Méran.' In 1819, Villefort expressed wish for violent dangerous diseases for honor of cure. Servant whispered urgent business; Villefort rose, quitted room. Returned, face beaming with delight. Renée regarded him with fond affection; handsome features lit with fire and animation seemed formed to excite admiration. Madame de Saint-Méran extended dry bony hand to Villefort, who imprinted respectful salute while looking at Renée.

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery and wedding**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding (1 February 1833, church of Saint-Paul): Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and Marius' suspicion**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade, heard frightful pistol shot behind Rue Mondétour.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and estrangement**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed from _thou_ to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. Still loved him sincerely. One day chanced to say "father." "Say Jean"—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean" with laughter. "That is right," said he. Turned aside to wipe eyes. This was the last time. Complete extinction ensued. At bottom, Cosette sincerely attached to man she long called father; but loved her husband still more dearly.

**Jean Valjean's withdrawal and death vigil**: Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** Head craned forward; chin moved; folds in gaunt neck painful to behold. Later confined to apartment, then bed. **[Lamentable cries heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** Marius and Cosette discovered all Jean Valjean had done; invited him back. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made from trade. Also managed very well with glass goods rivalling Berlin jewellery. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** Final decline: breath intermittent; found difficulty moving forearm; feet lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb increased, all majesty of soul displayed and spread over brow. Light of unknown world already visible in eyes. **In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and exposure**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** **Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's confrontation and evidence**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15th June, 1832: Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. "You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead. **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**
